thread_title: Hypothesis: Sarr. color forms are mostly of hybrid origin
breadcrumb: Hypothesis: Sarr. color forms are mostly of hybrid origin

posts.body_html:
A very interesting element in all this is, red colouration perpetually seems more emotionally compelling to we humans and, ipso facto, more noteworthy for many than what is thereby assumed to be foundational green in a species such as S. flava.

Whilst not necessarily apples with apples, perhaps worth considering for a moment are species that throw colour mutations such as the Leopard and Jaguar, each of which produces melanistic morphs, and the many birds that produce both melanistic and leucistic morphs, for easy examples. While none of these expressions are due to hybridisation and the morphs can be thrown from normal looking parents, a mating including a colour morph individual is more likely (but not exclusively) to result in the production of offspring expressing the mutation.

Perhaps rather than the green based S. flava forms being antecedent to the smaller numbers of red forms, what we see in the field simply reflects the predominance by weight of numbers of the green based forms. As is the predominance of the typically spotted version of the leopard. In turn, that predominance in S. flava potentially reflects a selected for advantage.

I suspect the red flava so closely associated with or actually within the non-red populations (or more accurately, the green ones with a solid red throat in W. Florida) indicate the red ones are a simple expressions of mutations that perpetuate due to the numbers of offspring produced (ie, we see stands of red expression), numbers over and above those of the animal species mentioned. Indeed, in W. Florida the red plants often have a red throat as in the green ones. In terms of colour alone as a factor, they are simply red rather than green.

Personally, I’ve never found favour with theory the solid red throat of an S. flava is the result of hybridisation with representations of S. purpurea that have a red throat. Any more than I do with the reverse. Rather, I suspect a circumstance of a similar successful trait having been selected for; a case of an apomorphy shared by the two species while not found in other Sarracenia species that are derived from the same foundational ancestor as S. flava.

Certainly, we simply don’t know what the evolutionary precursors of the Sarracenia we humans have known within approximately the last 14,000 years looked like. Inherently, in the case of S. flava the colour expressions are within a significant spectrum. I suspect the expression of red has always existed in the species itself, independent of interbreeding with other species. Veinless (not antho-free) and other colour expressions in S. purpurea are possibly a corollary.

Obviously hybrids with associated other species of Sarracenia occur in S. flava populations and hybridisation may indeed be a factor in red flava expressions. Who knows? For my money that would need to be proved in satisfactory empirical fashion across all wild populations. In alignment with sunbelle's statements and questioning, I'm not convinced that the explanation lies in the realm of theoretical hybridism.

posts.body_html:
One piece of anecdotal evidence is the lack of color forms of flava in South Georgia. This overlaps with the gap in the purpurea/rosea range. Go to the red hills of Thomasville, the Okeefenokee, or the Turner County Bog near Macon, you'll find nice stands of flava but not much variation. They are all rugelli. To my knowledge, the only color varieties in GA come from the Eastern part of the state near Savanna. The Bulloch County ornata is an example. A nice population of purpurea lies about 20 miles away. Near Tallahassee, flavas start picking up color with rubricorperas, ornatas, and cupreas. Not surprisingly, rosea grows in these parts.

Growing up around S. minor in the wild, I've been disappointed there hasn't been much attention to this species. There are all sorts of color forms. Heavily veined forms, some with very bulbous heads covered in areoles all around, some with dark red pitchers with pointed lids, and others with round lids with a red underside. Of course I'd expect variation in any species, but where are the Sarracenia minor var. ornata or Sarracenia minor var. rubrioperculata? I'm not proposing we start varietal names, but I do think the names applied to S. flava and alata do suggest some bias towards giving fancy Latin names to the big flashy trumpets. I will say that many of those heavily veined S. minor have faint red splotches on their petals, perhaps suggesting hybridization with S. psittacina.

Rambling aside, these are only personal observations and of course not extensive research. The Sarracenia species diverged so recently I don't have much problem with the idea floating around that the whole genus is a hybrid swarm. In any case, seeing subtle differences in the Sarracenia you encounter in different geographic locations is an interesting research area in itself. I agree more field work needs to be done. Let's just hope we leave enough fields to work in.

posts.body_html:
In Turner Co GA, Thomas Co, GA Colquitt Co, GA, and the Southeastern corner of GA (ie. known populations of S. flava var. rugelii that don't have any red forms) I'm not sure S. purpurea venosa or S. rosea exists in the extant populations or historically existed within "pollinating distance" of the flava rugelii populations. Can anyone confirm?

Let's also not forget, there are populations in Florida that have both S. rosea and S. flava and naczii hybrids, but no red form flavas. Same can be said about the Evans Co, GA/Tattnall Co, GA Sarracenia population: flava rugelii and purpurea venosa exist, but aside from catesbaei hybrids, there currently are no reports of any red flavas there. Let me add that the flava rugelii population in Evans Co, GA is very small and may just be a relic patch of a once larger population.

Interestingly, once you get to Bulloch Co, GA, then you start seeing historical records of S. purpurea ssp. venosa somewhat near that vicinity. I've seen ornatas there in sites that no longer exist, but the closest red forms I know of to that area are in Berkeley Co, SC.

None of this proves anything, but if the aforementioned information is verified, it does make much more compelling hypothesis.

An old purpurea herbarium specimen (likely rosea) exists from just west of Tifton. This isn't too far from the Turner County population ~20 miles north. Tifton is also about 30 miles north of my hometown where I saw rugeli but no others

The only other rosea is Randolf County (Southeast of Sumter). You can find it on the UGA online herbarium. I think the mention of the Tift County rosea is from a 1978 DNR publication on the Natural Environments of Georgia.

I also believe undersampling is a problem. The area has been an agricultural area and the Tifton uplands have little virgin soil left. Any idea if rugeli is just more adaptable? I find it easier to grow in cultivation.

For fun, I've been looking at atropurpurea flowers from various clones and inspecting them inside and out. What I'm finding very interesting is that those plants that appear to have pure yellow petals from the outside as the variant is described actually aren't pure yellow! The underside of the petals of all the atro. clones I've looked at so far have red pigments on them! Add this detail to everything else mentioned in this thread, and it's more evidence pointing towards hybridzation.




Here's a flower from S. Waccamaw, flowers fits the technical description of atropurpurea:



But lift up that petal and there's some pigments underneath it, suggesting past hybridization:



An atropurpurea from Okaloosa Co, FL, appears to be a very typical yellow flower on the outside:


But clearly pigmented on the inside:


And here's a "real" carolina atropurpurea clone's flower:


And again, the red pigments on the underside of the petals:

They don't tend to blush into red either and seem more like they bleed out from the veins until they're fully red. Hard to explain haha

For sure, it proves nothing by itself, but a pattern is emerging: individual clones of rubricorpora, some flava var. flava, many flava var. rugelii's, all atropurpureas I've ever seen, ornatas, cupreas, and probably even more have these pigments on the underside of the petals.

Plants that appear to be pure species aren't likely pure (ie. many rugelii clones), and this makes sense since outcrossing is favored in the wild. My homie Mike Wilder also made a very deep observation: the timeframe for speciation is likely in the 1000's of years and probably not as measurable in decades or hundreds of years. In other words, what I can observe in 3 generations of breeding in cultivation may have little implication of exactly what's going on in the wild compared to the effects of cross pollination over dozens of generations.

posts.body_html:
All this talk of introgression makes me think a sequencing experiment would be really helpful--see which regions of the genome look like they belong to one species and which regions belong to other species. A phylogenomics approach might bring a conclusion much faster than years of breeding experiments (though it might be more expensive). To my knowledge, there are no published Sarr genomes, though there some RNA-seq experiments.


Say you have "control" flava and roseas. You could sequence those as a reference and then sequence the red flava you suspect to be introgressed. If you identify chunks of the genome that look more like the rosea than the flava reference, that would be convining evidence of introgression as a source of color forms. Of course, for statistical strength you would probably have to look over many populations to show an association between introgression (or mutations) and color variants.

Hi Mike:

This is something we have been working on for over 20 years with several generations of controlled crosses. We're close to reporting our results but I should mention, and will mention in our paper, that the original suggestion (hypothesis) that red S. flava morphs came from S. rosea or S. purpurea was suggested by Fred Case. Stay tuned for our results.

Best,

Phil
